From Scott Armstrong and Julia Kempe: Formalization of De Giorgi--Nash--Moser Theory in Lean https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05984
repo: https://github.com/scottnarmstrong/DeGiorgi (56k lines)
blog post: https://www.scottnarmstrong.com/2026/04/formalizing-de-giorgi-nash-moser-theory-in-lean/

X post

@KempeLab and I just vibe-coded a Lean 4 formalization of elliptic De Giorgi–Nash–Moser theory. This is a cornerstone of modern elliptic PDE: local boundedness, weak Harnack, Harnack, and Hölder regularity for weak solutions with merely bounded measurable coefficients.

Looks like the authors audited the code:

So our confidence in the final result does not come from “the AI told us so.” It comes from the fact that we understand De Giorgi-Nash-Moser very well, and we repeatedly checked the formal statements against that understanding whenever something smelled wrong.

The author also said:

This is a very different picture of formalization than the mathlib ideal of "build a perfect library" This is why I think, for analysis, we may also need a parallel, messier approach. More a jungle, less a sculpted, curated garden.

In fact, before starting, we asked Claude how long a project like this should take. Its answer was basically: for a small team of dedicated and experienced Lean programmers, 2–4 years. That sounded completely plausible to me.
Instead, we did it in about two weeks. And yes, I really do mean vibe-coded: no human hand actually touched the Lean files. We used our LLMs subscriptions under supervision, supplied detailed proof blueprints, and intervened if they got stuck or made errors (by yelling at them).
Our point is NOT that LLMs can autonomously formalize hard mathematics. Our point is that the barrier to entry has changed, dramatically and very recently. Serious formalization in analysis and other areas of math is now much more accessible than many seem to realize.
Analysts should stop standing on the sidelines. Lean and Mathlib are fantastic, and with current LLMs it is now possible to bring serious modern analysis into the ecosystem much faster than I would have guessed even a few months ago.

Do you think the 2–4 years estimate is accurate?

IMHO 2-4 is slightly pessimistic, but that's a minor point. What strucks me here are two authors who admittedly don't know how to code in Lean and have developed an opinion about Mathlib to the point of suggesting how it should advance "for analysis". I'm not saying that the opinion is necessarily wrong, but that some hybris seems floating around.

I don't know what level of proficiency counts as "knowing how to code in Lean" but to me this sounds that they are quite confident in their Lean knowledge:

we repeatedly checked the formal statements against that understanding whenever something smelled wrong
This seems to be a completely pointless project. It seems to be very well-known result that nobody doubted and nothing at all can be reused (they are even proud of how messy it is).

This is also the new normal. We can add it to the pile of pointless projects and eventually there will be 10 times as many lines of pointless projects as there is mathlib, and then later on 100 times. Maybe 100x is only 1 year away? People have been asking how to "10x mathlib" for a while now but maybe they are going to accept "10x the amount of Lean code" and mathlib is going to have to try to figure out what, if anything, can be salvaged from the aftermath of this tsunami.

From the blog post (emphasis mine):

Formalizing mathematics in Lean is a very exciting development and Mathlib is already a fantastic project. But analysts, and especially PDE people, have mostly been watching from the sidelines. Part of the reason is obvious: modern analysis looks like exactly the kind of subject that ought to be painful to formalize. There are many layers of infrastructure, a lot of quantitative bookkeeping, and very few explicit formulas to hide behind. We have to carry around measurability certificates, almost-everywhere statements, admissible test functions, and so on. If one had asked me not long ago whether a project like this was realistic, I would probably have said yes in principle, but only with a large investment of time and a very experienced Lean team. (As recently as January I gave it serious thought and decided it was NOT realistic.)
...
One goal of this project was therefore simply to jump-start more analysis in Lean. I think a lot of analysts have had the feeling that formalization is exciting, that Mathlib is impressive, but that “our part of mathematics” is still too far away. At least from this experiment, I do not think that is true anymore.

Once we had Lean code compiling that certified our theorems, we still had a huge mess. There were many vestigial lemmas no longer needed, duplicate lemmas, and the compiler generated 739 “linter warnings” complaining that our code was not elegant. Some of our largest lean files had 10k lines, which is much too long for an elegant code base (as our LLMs informed us). Our vibe-coded code was disgusting, so we spent the last few days just cleaning the code. To be precise, we yelled at the LLMs to clean the code.
Most likely this part was done imperfectly, and we expect that Lean pros will still find our code lacking in elegance. (We did our best!)

Patrick Massot said:

This seems to be a completely pointless project. It seems to be very well-known result that nobody doubted and nothing at all can be reused (they are even proud of how messy it is).

I’m not sure I fully agree with this. As the post itself notes, the example is somewhat toy in nature, but it still demonstrates that modern AI is already capable of formalizing results from contemporary PDE research papers. Not everyone prioritizes elegance or code quality; for someone who has just proved a theorem and wants immediate reassurance of its correctness, this kind of formalization will likely become quite standard. It’s not hard to imagine a near future in which many papers come with a quick, low-quality Lean formalization produced via vibe coding. I also imagine that two distinct styles of formalization will emerge. One is the more idealistic approach exemplified by Mathlib, where proofs are developed cleanly and systematically, with significant effort devoted to structure, reusability, and elegance. The other is a more messier and less reusable, but designed to rapidly test and validate results at the cutting edge of research.

Yongxi Lin (Aaron) said:

It’s not hard to imagine a near future in which many papers come with a quick, low-quality Lean formalization produced via vibe coding. I also imagine that two distinct styles of formalization will emerge. One is the more idealistic approach exemplified by Mathlib, where proofs are developed cleanly and systematically, with significant effort devoted to structure, reusability, and elegance. The other is a more messier and less reusable, but designed to rapidly test and validate results at the cutting edge of research.

This is certainly correct--and this will absolutely happen and is happening. Two points: (1) this will only last a short period of time (6 months? 1 year?) until the LLMs can also code it elegantly, too; (2) if we can formalize in Lean (even in an ugly way) and teach the AIs to do it, then we can use the AIs to prove theorems.

This will absolutely happen, and nobody (outside of this message board?) will care that it is not in mathlib or that the code is ugly!

Look, I understand some of the reactions to our work here, and I expected it. I am not stupid. I still find some of your reactions here a bit overboard, a bit sad, and bit hard to understand.

Suddenly Lean has the potential to actually become super important to a typical working research mathematician, and your reaction is to be pissed off? To call us arrogant and useless? Because barbarians are at your gates?

I would suggest a different approach!

@Scott Armstrong I don't know if I count amongst those who called you "arrogant" because I brought in some hybris, but let me clarify my point. For someone who's been thinking for a while about how should Sobolev spaces enter Mathlib, my impression is that analysis is perfectly fit for the library. Of course it will take a lot of time, but that was the case for almost everything else. I've got the feeling that your, and many of your colleagues' impression, that "analysis requires a different style of library" is at least partly misinformed and your adamant statement that you vibe-code the whole project confirmed my opinion. On the other hand, I share your vision that many many projects like yours will se the light in the very near future and I am excited to see that formal math is blossoming. But as a Mathlib maintainer this rises a lot of question, starting from how to react to a cascade of (code-wise) low-quality contributions to the future of this community, whose existence is quintessential for other projects to stand upon its shoulders.

I think what you did is very interesting, because it shows one can get into Lean without a lot of a priori knowledge, and this is needed for broader adoption by the community. But it's also true that there are concerns with the reusability of this kind of project. For instance, the statements in your project conform with the way we usually write statements in analysis: we write them on Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd, but in practice we're not afraid to apply them to R×R\R \times \RR×R, say, while this is not the same space formally.

A lesson that formalization has told us is that this is a real difficulty, and that statements should be written in the proper generality to be broadly applicable. So, all the statements in your formalization should probably be written assuming that E is a finite-dimensional inner-product real vector space, instead of sticking with EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d) -- or even, for some early definitions like HasWeakPartialDeriv, assuming a normed vector space. Otherwise, it means that anyone relying on your formalization will be also stuck in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd, and then if a whole ecosystem builds on your formalization we will get very interesting definitions and theorems but just in this restricted system. And then maybe one day someone will need to use it in a symplectic setting, working on R2×R2\R^2 \times \R^2R2×R2, and boom.

I wonder how we could improve on this situation. Register a file of good formalization practices for LLM, that we would encourage people doing vibe-coding to feed to their LLMs, and containing advice such as "in analysis, even if statements are given in Rd\R^dRd in a blueprint, formalize them on a general normed vector space or inner product vector space"?

Scott Armstrong said:

This is certainly correct--and this will absolutely happen and is happening. Two points: (1) this will only last a short period of time (6 months? 1 year?) until the LLMs can also code it elegantly, too; (2) if we can formalize in Lean (even in an ugly way) and teach the AIs to do it, then we can use the AIs to prove theorems.

This will absolutely happen, and nobody (outside of this message board?) will care that it is not in mathlib or that the code is ugly!

I guess I will say that people outside this message board should probably care regardless, because Mathlib is the foundational library imported by essentially all AI projects . This is true for human projects too, and for continued human usage the "cleanness" is important.

Additionally, IMO no one would stomach verifying definitions in a repo that begins by defining the natural numbers, or even running that much compute, having an increasing set of human verified and foundational mathematical objects is very invaluable for AI users.

Furthermore, it will eventually function as one of the more pristine sources to get quality Lean code to train such models, after all how would they be able to learn "cleaner" code without such a place.

Indeed if someone wanted to put Sobolev spaces into mathlib, it would be excellent!! This was the most annoying part of our project, that we had to essentially formalize half of Ch5 of Evans PDE book in order to even begin. Certainly Sobolev spaces should be in mathlib. A request: please formalize Sobolev spaces on bounded domains with weak derivatives in L^p, and not just on R^d using Fourier. Please!

I would love to see more analysis in Lean and in mathlib. But I am impatient and I want to prove the cool stuff. This is not even my day job, it's a side hussle, so I'm going to just vibe code stuff and make ugly code and be part of the Tsunami. Sorry!

My point that you are taking issue with is just this. Analysis is fundamentally about methods as opposed to results. If you are a student and you ask "ok, but has someone written down this estimate in this other setting/case" you will be told "no, of course no one has written down exactly that, you have to redo the estimates from scratch for that particular case but it's normal. The proof ideas are more or less the same. Sit down and do it." It is hard to even write reference books on this stuff! No matter what you write, someone will say it's not handling their case.

Anyway, I wanted to see De Giorgi-Nash-Moser formalized in my lifetime. How long should I wait for Sobolev spaces to appear? With Julia we realized that, hey, we can just do it.

Do you see my point? There are room for both approaches, and both are valuable.

I think the mathlib project is obviously fantastic, obviously important. I have been saying so for years. I have been told by people working in my subfield, after I explain to them what mathlib IS and what Lean IS (which I have to do, because most have essentially never heard of these things), that "oh but come on, they will never get to the point of formalizing something in PDE, like, say, De Giorgi-Nash-Moser." Several different people in different conversations have said that to me, using DGNM as their example!

A suggestion: you could decide that this is not an attack on mathlib, it is just a demonstration of the growing importance of mathlib!

One suggestion: the most effective way to get a theory X into mathlib is not to ask that someone please please add it and ask how long it'll take to magically appear, but to check the zulip archives for previous discussions about X, identify the smallest, most fundamental part of X that's missing in mathlib, and contribute that yourself. That also applies for X = Sobolev spaces

My vision is that such projects will become more and more frequent in the very near future. I am both afraid that they will grab attention away from mathlib and excited that they will inform us very concretely what areas are in most dire need of a mathlib formalisation.

I want to use AIs to help me prove theorems. As a first step, they have to be able to check their bullshit against reality, since they generate so much bullshit, and it seems Lean is the best way to do this. So I have to get the AI to first learn how to code in Lean. I want the code to compile sorry-free and certify the result, well enough that I can auto-generate feedback to the AIs. I have two comments about this:

  • My understanding is that your primary interest is in training AIs to help you in creating novel mathematics. And that the sustainability of the code you produced is thus no so crucial. In fact, it seems to me that you are not specially interested in contributing to or building on mathlib per se, and would be happy with an IA generating a proof of a theorem like De Giorgi-Nash-Moser from first principles. Other people here have a different motivation and agenda for formalizing mathematics using ITPs, rather aiming at building a coherent, future-proof library of formalized mathematics.

  • Auditing formal code is hard, even focussing only on statements, and it is becoming massively harder these days. A few years ago, proving the correctness of safety critical code was the only application in which reviewers would assume the formalizer to be adversarial. I personally know no example of a formal proof of a math statement that has become obsolete because of a bug discovered in the kernel of an ITP. But now things are different, and I would bet on IAs trying to cheat on any front, from making use of bugs in the kernel to tweaking elaboration, parsing, etc. (your paper has interesting comments about the training of elaboration by the way). As of today, I consider this as the most vulnerable part of Lean (and its fellow ITPs), specially in the context of formalized mathematics, which crucially relies on a complex notation apparatus.

I think mathlib is a very worthy project and if I had infinite time (and a matching skill set) I would be definitely interested in contributing to it! But I see myself as being better at other things, and probably should focus my attention elsewhere. Just because of who I am and my personality. So I doubt I will be contributing hand-written code to mathlib any time soon.

I believe - and hope - that both types of projects can exist in parallel without undermining each other.

Your points seem very worth considering. I have no answers on your second concern, about AIs cheating. Obviously a big concern in general, not just for Lean.

Sure, I would have a lot to say about the project. I am not sure how to type it all here. Here is a synopsis.

  1. We started with the idea of it taking my elliptic regularity notes (private latex file) and making a compiling lean code out of it. But I realized we needed Sobolev space precursors, so I asked the LLM to try to (i) put my latex notes into a very detailed "formalization outline" (in a markdown md file) with sub-md files devoted to each part. Then to also make a separate "Sobolev preliminaries" md file with a list of the Sobolev and measure theory precursors we would need. I told the LLM to figure out what was needed and to make a proof outline.

  2. Once those MD files were in good shape, we fed it to the agents like throwing meat to a hungry pack of wolves. This was a mistake, I would do it very differently now. Next time I do this I will be much more detailed in my planning.

  3. It immediately got stuck, and often at funny places. Sometimes at places a human would also get stuck. We asked it over and over "explain why you are stuck, what is the problem" and we would have a natural language conversation with it until it told us ok, now I understand, I will formalize it like that. Then it would succeed until it got stuck at the next point. There were some hilarious and unexpected problems that arose along the way, like the LLMs would change the statements of the lemmas to make them easier to prove.

Once there was any progress at all (a lemma got proved) we would have teams of rival agents audit the code. Usually if there was something wrong they would find it. At some point, after we kept asking for the proofs to be "sorry-free", it started introducing axioms. Then we improved our language to say "unconditionally, sorry-free and axiom-free" and scolded them.

  1. After three days we had finished the hardest single piece, which was the Sobolev extension theorem in the unit ball.

  2. After six days we had De Giorgi first L^infty estimate compiling unconditionally.

  3. Things more heavily stuck in the second half of the project, where elaboration issues started to become very burdensome. We had to launch teams of agents to run around the code trying to find places where it was compiling slowly, try to diagnose the problem and proposing fixes, etc. We figured out a "no EuclideanSpace" rule although the agents kept forgetting this.

Knowing what I know now, I think we could do the whole thing in 4-5 days and the code would be much better. Still not pristine mathlib-level code, but it's still only April 2026. Let's see what things look like in the summer.

On the whole we used only our personal LLM subscriptions. I used Claude and ChatGPT pro, so I pay $400/month. GPT5.4 is much better than Claude, so it does the hard parts, and Claude Opus 4.6 was used in a supplementary role. Of course they were not operating in my browser, but in my repo directory and the interaction was via VScode. In terms of literal cost it was in the hundreds (but not thousands) of US dollars.
Thanks!

Edward van de Meent said:

for the sake of completeness, how much time did you sink into your personal elliptic regularity notes?

A long time. Those were written by me over the years, mainly for my own consumption. A lot of it was written in 2019-2020 just before the pandemic, when I was obsessed with trying to understand how/why it is difficult to prove the optimal dependence of the Holder constant on the ellipticity ratio. Nobody had written this, to my knowledge, so I basically latexed every proof I could find of De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theory (all possible approaches) and tracked dependence on ellipticity explicitly. They were written in a very very compact/terse way, actually very suitable for formalization because of the style in which I like to write the proofs. Many of the proofs were told to me orally by Guido De Philippis, or he would direct me to the correct paper written by Italians in the 70s with the slickest argument.

They were unpolished and had typos everywhere. Just before launching I had ChatGPT run through the file and audit it carefully, complete some uncompleted lemmas and try to get rid of the typos, etc. The notes were only like 50 pages, so I would say dozens of hours but not hundreds? It depends on what you count, does sitting around thinking about elliptic regularity count? Then you have to count thousands of hours.
Right, so in total, if someone unfamiliar with the subject would have to do this formalization "from scratch", it might take thousands of hours, rather than just a few days.

I think a lot of reasonable general AI anxiety is being taken out on folks who come with goodwill and make respectful and well-modulated claims, and the negative response here is an instance of that. I would direct it instead at people who make unreasonable claims, or at AI companies that refuse to respect community norms. Or even better, channel it into designing better incentive systems and into better communicating what makes an elegant, reusable, handcrafted formalization valuable to different people for different reasons

FWIW the PL community went through this AI onslaught five years ago, and we came out the other side perfectly fine. It was scary to imagine we could have gone the route of NLP and gotten swallowed nearly whole, but there were ways to avoid this. I see a lot of remarks in this thread which mention the words "code quality". I have no objection to this: code quality matters!

However, while I think that comparisons of Mathlib to software and to old-school human literature are both valid and useful, it is the comparison to the latter which is more relevant. In other words, I claim that we have more to learn from Bourbaki than from Linux (though of course they both contain valuable lessons for us).

Furthermore, with Mathlib we impose quite different constraints on ourselves than the usual mathematical literature.

For example, the group algebra R[G]R[G]R[G] is a standard object that undergraduates meet in their representation theory course but, though they are seldom told this, they already met it when the studied polynomials R[t]R[t]R[t]. The only difference is that for polynomials , instead of the group GGG one has the natural numbers N\mathbb{N}N which are merely a monoid. So in fact the group algebra and polynomials are both instances of this same definition. In Mathlib we try very hard to unify such definitions and so instead of the group algebra we have docs#MonoidAlgebra. And actually that's not even the end of the story --- we needed to construct free non-associative algebras so we actually further generalised to the magma algebra (though perhaps confusingly we kept the name "monoid algebra").

I mention this example because for me it highlights two ways AI-assisted development might change things:

  1. To date, we have tried very hard to unify concepts, partly because it obviates the need for us to spend time repeating ourselves. Maybe if repeating ourselves becomes very cheap, this calculus changes?
  2. Mathlib is absolutely stuffed with unifications like the one above which require taking a somewhat panoramic view of mathematics. If we want AIs to do this too, we need more than just local code quality rules of thumb.
To what extent can that blueprint be turned into a suite of Lean tactics? (I'm way outside my mathematical comfort zone, asking this question.)

I think most of the arguments in this thread and elsewhere stems from two (or perhaps three) different crowds talking. They have common language - Lean- but different goals and methods.

1st crowd (mathlib community) looks at Lean bottom-to-top: unified, reusable, modular code. Current research would be great to formalize but it's not a must. Bourbaki-style approach to mathematics taken to code.

2nd crowd (let's call them 'non-coding mathematicians') looks at Lean top-to-bottom: it's all about formalizing current research to support existing mathematicians' work and push it forward. Lean is a side tool for discovery plus verification. Code can be messy, it just have to work.

At some point these crowds will meet, it's just not today, because of various gaps. Finally one might argue there's a 3rd crowd coming from AI / ex-academics (me included), that care mostly about verified reasoning and how to make machines think better. Cares about research, but needs reusability to make the new generation of LLMs reliably better.
